For the better part of the last century, my grandfather, Roberto Piontelli, a scientist, collected thousands of books.

His collection was carefully catalogued by my grandmother, Edvige Tonolli. One by one, she captured the information on an index card.

The cards behind the story

Original pages.
New perspectives.

The family catalogue contains 49,780 scanned records, including books, papers, volumes, continuation cards and cross-references. This is not a count of distinct physical books.

The close views use original catalogue scans. The final field contains one square for each scanned catalogue record.

The timeline places all 49,780 catalogue records into columns of individual squares. There are 33,971 records with a detected year. Dates may refer to an edition, a cited work or a serial range. The remaining 15,809 records have no detected year.

Publication geography. Each white square is one catalogue record. Imprint-like place names are read from the original card transcriptions, with medium confidence; this is not a complete publication census. Countries use modern boundaries. Cards with no clear place stay in “Place unknown”; cards naming more than one country stay in “Multiple countries” and are counted only once. Continuations, cross-references and ambiguous places are left unlocated. The map does not infer a location from an author’s nationality. Closely spaced stacks are offset with lines back to the country to keep the squares visible.

Country outlines: Natural Earth, 1:110m Admin 0 ↗. The source uses de facto boundaries. Borders are a present-day geographic reference, not a claim about the historical edition.

The story of the collection and its cataloguing comes from the family. The cards shown are original scans. The wall animates transcribed text from the original catalogue cards; it is an illustration of the work, not a recording of Edvige at her typewriter.

Typing-time estimate. An illustration of the work, not a recorded duration. 49,780 scanned records × 2 minutes = about 1,659 hours. That is 207 eight-hour days, 41 five-day weeks, or about 10 working months. This assumes one typed card per scanned record and excludes reading, research, sorting, corrections and breaks.
